key_findings.finding: For a confirmed acute proximal lower-extremity DVT when therapeutic anticoagulation is temporarily/absolutely contraindicated by a recent intracranial hemorrhage or craniotomy, guideline-consistent management is urgent multidisciplinary evaluation for a temporary/retrievable inferior vena cava (IVC) filter to reduce pulmonary-embolism risk, with mechanical prophylaxis and serial reassessment; this is treatment of established VTE, not routine primary prophylaxis. Recent neurosurgery and intracranial hemorrhage are documented real-world indications, and trauma consensus specifically identifies proximal DVT or PE with contraindicated therapeutic anticoagulation as a highly selective filter indication.

source_tools.relevance: Review summarizing guideline indication as lower-limb VTE plus absolute anticoagulation contraindication

key_findings.finding: The filter should not be viewed as equivalent to anticoagulation: PREPIC evidence found fewer pulmonary emboli but more recurrent DVT and no survival benefit over long follow-up; PREPIC2 found no reduction in recurrent PE when a retrievable filter was added to anticoagulation. Therefore, use the filter only while anticoagulation is unsafe, establish a retrieval/follow-up plan, and start therapeutic anticoagulation (often initially reversible UFH when neurosurgery agrees) as soon as repeat brain imaging and clinical stability permit, followed by standard therapy.

In this patient four days after evacuation of a subdural hematoma, therapeutic UFH, LMWH, DOACs, and warfarin should not be started empirically while the intracranial bleeding risk remains prohibitive; UFH is preferred only when anticoagulation is later judged acceptable because it has a short half-life and can be stopped/reversed, not because it is safe during the current contraindication. DOACs and warfarin are unsuitable immediate choices because they are less readily titratable/reversible in this early postoperative setting; LMWH is also therapeutic anticoagulation and carries intracranial rebleeding risk.

source_tools.relevance: Early therapeutic anticoagulation after craniotomy is a specific safety/timing concern

key_findings.finding: Catheter-directed thrombolysis/systemic thrombolysis is inappropriate for ordinary DVT here because recent intracranial hemorrhage and neurosurgery are major/near-absolute bleeding contraindications. Catheter thrombectomy or surgical venous thrombectomy is not routine substitute therapy; reserve it for exceptional limb-threatening iliofemoral obstruction/phlegmasia or selected cases after vascular, interventional, and neurosurgical review, because the procedure and adjunctive lytics/anticoagulation may still provoke bleeding.

source_tools.relevance: Evidence search identified thrombolysis as carrying intracranial-hemorrhage risk and interventional treatment as selective
Pharmacomechanical thrombolysis literature concerns patients with relative contraindications, not this very recent intracranial bleed

key_findings.finding: Aspirin does not treat acute DVT and is not an adequate alternative to therapeutic anticoagulation or an IVC filter. Observation alone is acceptable only if duplex shows an isolated distal calf DVT and the patient can undergo close serial ultrasound surveillance; it is not appropriate for confirmed proximal DVT, propagation, pulmonary embolism, or severe symptoms. The immediate bedside steps are confirmatory duplex ultrasound, assess for PE/hemodynamic instability and limb threat, notify neurosurgery/vascular or interventional radiology, use intermittent pneumatic compression if safe, and repeat head imaging to define when anticoagulation can be resumed.

source_tools.relevance: DVT-treatment guidance distinguishes proximal from isolated distal DVT and notes limited evidence for isolated distal disease
Mechanical prophylaxis is used when intracranial hemorrhage contraindicates anticoagulation
